COVID: Impact on the Local Economy

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Could the economic impact of coronavirus in South Africa be more deadly than the virus itself?

Unique Selling Point:
It is all good and well to declare Coronavirus a National Disaster and order business and people to stay at home and practice social distancing, but how is this going to affect small businesses and self employed people, who in South Africa are a major sector working class?

Summary:
How is the imminent Lockdown and social distancing going to affect, the lives and livelihoods of South Africans.

How is Coronavirus affecting the local economy and it’s impact on our current recession?
What role is the National Command Council, set up as part of the national state of disaster, going to play in averting what could be disastrous for South Africa?

It is all good and well to declare Coronavirus a National Disaster and order business and people to stay at home and practice social distancing, but how is this going to affect small businesses and self employed people, who in South Africa are a major sector working class?

We look at the chain of employment and sustainability of workers that could potentially explode into an unimaginable situation.

Experts say the economic impact of coronavirus could be more deadly than the virus itself.

Restaurants now have regulated hours, they can’t have more than 40 people at a time, Parkhurst and Rosebank for example, on Saturday this week, were ghost towns. Waiters who work in these places depend on tips to make a living. If they are not going to work then the taxi industry is impacted, who also depend on fares to earn a wage for themselves and the taxi owners.

Further information:
Driving around Johannesburg at the weekend, the city was lifeless.

Gyms are closing down, many gym trainers pay the gym’s a monthly fee like R9000,00 per month, which they can only pay if they have clients to train. The Clients are freezing their gym accounts, but the trainers in some of these facilities are being asked to pay only 50% of their fees, but without clients, even this is not sustainable.

There are people who depend on a living through weekly markets where they sell their wares, these markets are now being closed down.

Those who are self employed are unable to sustain their businesses if they depend on client contact to earn money, eg, music teachers, etc..

We speak to people who’s incomes are already being compromised because of this, and it’s only the beginning.

The question is, what happens when money starts running out, and people don’t have money to buy food, pay for electricity etc. Already people’s purses were stretched with the current recession and economic outlook. This could lead to looting and increased opportunistic crime, what is the Government Disaster fund doing to mitigate this? Have they set aside food packages that can be dropped off in areas where people may be starving, what is going to happen when people can’t afford to pay their electricity because their income has been stifled, how is Eskom’s current debt burden going to cope with this? We can try and get an interview with the President on this, who is the Chairperson of the Disaster Management Fund, or someone else that is suitable.

Other countries like in the UK and Germany are allowing their citizens state help money, eg in Ireland they are receiving around $240 pounds a week, in South Africa we are in a recession with limited funds available for anything, the State cannot afford to help the ordinary citizen weather this storm, how is this going to play out in the poor communities who already have little if no assistance?

Even criminals are going to find it harder to do certain crimes, with businesses closed down and people staying at home, it’s going to make burglaries harder, and therefore there may even be an increase in violent crime, even the amount of cars on the roads are reduced, and this will impede the way criminals operate which may give rise to a different type of crime wave. What is SAPS doing to secure communities in such eventualities?

Mike Shussler warns, that the South African economy could shrink by a further 5% due to the measures taken around the world and in South Africa to combat the Covid 19 Pandemic, this would also lead to an increase in unemployment from an already high rate. Tourism in the Western Cape will be worst hit. The impact on Restaurants, hotels, Uber and Bolt drivers, thousands of people who normally make money for themselves may not be able to because of the pandemic. Wholesalers supplying to restaurants will take a hit, nursery schools will also lose money.

The plus side of this is that pharmaceutical companies and food companies are flourishing.

Professor Neil Rankin form Stellenbosch says, “real time data, suggests that sales are down by between 20% and 50% now, and that’s likely to get worse. “

There is also a prediction, that the worldwide impact could outdo the Great Depression of the 1920’s. This will affect South Africa even further because of our dependence on global economic links.

Press Release:


Lockdown is here. South Africans have been ordered to stay at home for three weeks. With job losses, the informal sector collapsing, businesses closing and only essential services allowed, the COVID-19 disaster is not only a public health crisis but an economic one too.

Script:


LINK: South Africa is in lockdown –

LINK: The National Command Council’s strategy to try and flatten the curve of Covid-19 infection.

VO: In response, many South Africans chose to think about the future in present terms - perhaps just for the next 21 days. Those who could afford it, went shopping in droves, stockpiling and cleaning out the shelves, whilst social distancing became immaterial // and despite warnings from government against price hiking, many items were at a premium, taking advantage of fearful consumers. Frustrations were shared in social media outrage.

Sound up: We're standing by the door for 45 minutes, they're putting a price increase.

VO: The first night of lockdown saw 19 arrests in Johannesburg, as the police, metro police and private security enforced the new law.

Police on Streets sound up: No alcohol in the car, no cooler box.

VO: And the army has taken to the streets - all this, in an attempt to avert a human catastrophe that could cost South Africa thousands of lives.

LINK: But we may be facing another disaster, an economic one.

MIKE: There will be many businesses that will be victims in this viral slaughter field*

Duma: We need to talk about not just flattening the curve of the disease also flattening the curve of the recession

LINK: This could take us down a spiral that directly affects our livelihoods, and not just in the present, the aftermath may be long lasting.

VO: Economist Mike Schussler points out that 21 days of lockdown, means the South African economy will be virtually at a standstill, for 6% of the year.
Mike: One could even call it a depression environment of say a double digit decline in our economy of 10 or 11, 12 percent.

VO: On the 23rd of March President Ramaphosa announced measures not only for slowing the spread of COVID-19 but also interventions designed to support peoples’ livelihoods, which include wage subsidies, tax relief for low income earners and relaxed tax payment schedules for SMEs under R50 million annual turnover. Economist Duma Gqubule, is of the opinion that the full package of interventions is not enough to protect an already exposed economy.

Duma: Do the maths, we are going to take two thirds of our GDP off line for one quarter and it will never get up to speed so that's six hundred or eight hundred billion rands out of the economy and you're giving us a two billion rand fund. We're going to have a decline that is three to four times more than what happened after the global financial crisis. We could see two million jobs lost.

VO: For workers who qualify, 30 billion rands has been made available through the Unemployment insurance fund.

Mike : When you get unemployment insurance, it's never enough. It's only a portion of your salary and a very small ceiling to it.

Duma: All the other initiatives from governments are way too small, 200 million rands in a Tourism Fund and also 3 billion rands from the IDC. All of that doesn't add up to anything that's going to stabilize our economy.

VO: Tourism and the hospitality industries were already hard hit, and for smaller operators like Tosca Korver who manages a boutique hotel in Cape Town, reserves are minimal.

Tosca: Well on Monday we received our last cancellation so we have zero bookings going forward We've got a rainy day fund that we can keep going for about a month but after that hopefully this is either over or we have to close doors.

VO: Hotels are just one sector of the economy suddenly left with no customers.

Mike: Passenger travel by air, by train., restaurants, petrol stations. We're seeing a whole host of places really struggling with this. And obviously the uncertainty that this creates means that people are less likely to buy durable goods such as houses, cars, furniture in this environment.

VO: Even before lockdown, the Eventing and Exhibitions sector took strain. Projeni Pather is the Chairperson of the Association of African Exhibition Organisers, whose responsibility is to ensure that the industry thrives and grows.

Projeni: We did a survey just at the beginning of the week and we looked at the economic impact in just about 160 respondents that replied and that's close to about a 1 billion rand revenue loss already.

Claire: What exhibitions or shows or expos have been canceled.

Progeni: Big ones that are coming up would be World Travel Market which is supposed to be in Cape Town next month and then we have Tourism Indaba which is supposed to be in Durban in May. And those attract international exhibitors, international visitors. If you look at the number of companies that are impacted by that, it's those businesses that are looking for a platform to grow their businesses and the different industry sectors, those businesses obviously affect the economy as a whole. So the ripple effect is enormous.

Link: Parkhurst in Johannesburg is renowned as a social hub for restaurant, pub and coffee shop goers. On the eve of lockdown, it already feels like a dead zone as businesses prepare to shut down.

VO: Restaurateur James Diack is closing his doors. He owns 4 eateries around Johannesburg.

James: Just because our doors are shut, it doesn't mean that our costs have stopped We are a cash flow business,

Claire: What have you communicated to your staff members, lots of anxiety going around?

James: We've run a full payroll for this month. And then once we're back up and running, we will do our best to work with them we are all uncertain, we don't know where this ends.

VO: Wendy Alberts, CEO of the Restaurant Association of South Africa has already been coordinating efforts to support the restaurant industry across the country.

Wendy: Engagements that I'm going to have in the very next few days and weeks are gonna be very real conversations that we need to have with government and the landlords to put a financial plan relooking the entire financial ability of a lease agreement. Every restaurant will pay a percentage of turnover to the landlord. It means that the landlord is also playing a responsibility in driving feet through the doors in rebuilding their centers, in rebuilding those businesses.

VO: Although the banks are coming to the party, with payment holidays for small businesses and student loans, there are more pressing issues for the man in the street, like rents, home loans and car repayments.

Duma: I do not think we're going to see mass repossessions of people's cars and houses and so on.

VO: Payment holidays for individual consumers have not yet been implemented, but some banks are encouraging customers to engage on a case by case basis.

Albert Mashimbi owns one taxi and already he is not sure where his next paycheck is coming from.

Albert: If normally in the morning the taxi takes three loads of people, it is no longer three loads. Just one load in the morning and one in the evening. We need to speak to the bank, so that our cars don't get taken

Claire: Do you think your business will survive?

Albert: No it’s not going to survive.

VO: Philemon Mulaudzi, Chairperson of the Northern Taxi Liaison Committee is worried.

Philemon: We don't have any plan. We will see if the government can assist us or maybe the government if they can talk to the banks. Maybe they can give us a little bit of money just to cover the cost over the months.

VO: As global markets collapse under the strain of COVID-19, South Africa is not exempt from the fallout. Already in a recession and with foreign investment curtailed, now that Moody's has cut South Africa’s credit rating to junk, economic recovery could be even tougher.

Duma: All the problems we have in society, they've just been fast forwarded in terms of you know the D-day for us as a country. So Eskom is going to have serious troubles over the next six months in terms of their financing.

VO: On the plus side, with a slump in demand for electricity during lockdown, Eskom expects no load shedding and they are able to do short term maintenance and repairs to improve generation capacity. But other SOE's may fall by the wayside.

Mike: There's no way that SAA or SA Express can survive under these circumstances.

VO: And on Friday SA Express Business Rescue practitioners filed for liquidation.

Mike: There might not even be a Prasa after this. So it's going to be a very sort of big social experiment that we've never seen before.

Duma: We have to think innovatively So let's just say we're going to do an 800 billion stimulus.

VO: According to Duma Gqubule the stimulus could come from various sources like foreign exchange reserves of about 800 billion rands, interest rate cuts, and surpluses in the Public Investment Corporation as well as the UIF.

Duma : Let's look at the whole balance sheet of South Africa and not just focus on liabilities there's also the assets that we have as a country.

VO: As the country locks down in eerie silence and shuts off for the next three weeks, how will one of the world's most unequal societies cope in unprecedented times?

Piatt - Bmi UCM1025 Mysterious Murder Background 2 00:00:20 ATOMICA ONE PUBLISHING - ASCAP Matthias Fluor - Suisa UCM1080 Innermost Fears Underscore Background 24 00:00:19 DNA MUSIK Tony Delmonte, Alan Jay Reed MAM054 Your Time Is Up Background 5 00:00:16 DNA MUSIK Tony Delmonte, Sebastian Watzinger MAM054 Invert Locker Background 1 00:00:12 EXTREME MUSIC LIBRARY LTD (PRS) Mel Wesson, Nineoneone XCD524 Remain Silent Background 43 00:00:11 ATOMICA ONE PUBLISHING - ASCAP Eric Palmer - Ascap UCM1006 Puzzle Box Background 20 00:00:11 ATOMICA ONE PUBLISHING - ASCAP Matthias Fluor - Suisa UCM1080 Smoking Out Intentions Background 50 00:00:11 ATOMICA ONE PUBLISHING - ASCAP Timothy Hosman - Ascap MNL1032 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 29 March 2020 - Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 01 April 2020 Press Release: Lockdown is here. South Africans have been ordered to stay at home for three weeks. With job losses, the informal sector collapsing, businesses closing and only essential services allowed, the COVID-19 disaster is not only a public health crisis but an economic one too. Script: LINK: South Africa is in lockdown – LINK: The National Command Council’s strategy to try and flatten the curve of Covid-19 infection. VO: In response, many South Africans chose to think about the future in present terms - perhaps just for the next 21 days. Those who could afford it, went shopping in droves, stockpiling and cleaning out the shelves, whilst social distancing became immaterial // and despite warnings from government against price hiking, many items were at a premium, taking advantage of fearful consumers. Frustrations were shared in social media outrage. Sound up: We're standing by the door for 45 minutes, they're putting a price increase. VO: The first night of lockdown saw 19 arrests in Johannesburg, as the police, metro police and private security enforced the new law. Police on Streets sound up: No alcohol in the car, no cooler box. VO: And the army has taken to the streets - all this, in an attempt to avert a human catastrophe that could cost South Africa thousands of lives. LINK: But we may be facing another disaster, an economic one. MIKE: There will be many businesses that will be victims in this viral slaughter field* Duma: We need to talk about not just flattening the curve of the disease also flattening the curve of the recession LINK: This could take us down a spiral that directly affects our livelihoods, and not just in the present, the aftermath may be long lasting. VO: Economist Mike Schussler points out that 21 days of lockdown, means the South African economy will be virtually at a standstill, for 6% of the year. Mike: One could even call it a depression environment of say a double digit decline in our economy of 10 or 11, 12 percent. VO: On the 23rd of March President Ramaphosa announced measures not only for slowing the spread of COVID-19 but also interventions designed to support peoples’ livelihoods, which include wage subsidies, tax relief for low income earners and relaxed tax payment schedules for SMEs under R50 million annual turnover. Economist Duma Gqubule, is of the opinion that the full package of interventions is not enough to protect an already exposed economy. Duma: Do the maths, we are going to take two thirds of our GDP off line for one quarter and it will never get up to speed so that's six hundred or eight hundred billion rands out of the economy and you're giving us a two billion rand fund. We're going to have a decline that is three to four times more than what happened after the global financial crisis. We could see two million jobs lost. VO: For workers who qualify, 30 billion rands has been made available through the Unemployment insurance fund. Mike : When you get unemployment insurance, it's never enough. It's only a portion of your salary and a very small ceiling to it. Duma: All the other initiatives from governments are way too small, 200 million rands in a Tourism Fund and also 3 billion rands from the IDC. All of that doesn't add up to anything that's going to stabilize our economy. VO: Tourism and the hospitality industries were already hard hit, and for smaller operators like Tosca Korver who manages a boutique hotel in Cape Town, reserves are minimal. Tosca: Well on Monday we received our last cancellation so we have zero bookings going forward We've got a rainy day fund that we can keep going for about a month but after that hopefully this is either over or we have to close doors. VO: Hotels are just one sector of the economy suddenly left with no customers. Mike: Passenger travel by air, by train., restaurants, petrol stations. We're seeing a whole host of places really struggling with this. And obviously the uncertainty that this creates means that people are less likely to buy durable goods such as houses, cars, furniture in this environment. VO: Even before lockdown, the Eventing and Exhibitions sector took strain. Projeni Pather is the Chairperson of the Association of African Exhibition Organisers, whose responsibility is to ensure that the industry thrives and grows. Projeni: We did a survey just at the beginning of the week and we looked at the economic impact in just about 160 respondents that replied and that's close to about a 1 billion rand revenue loss already. Claire: What exhibitions or shows or expos have been canceled. Progeni: Big ones that are coming up would be World Travel Market which is supposed to be in Cape Town next month and then we have Tourism Indaba which is supposed to be in Durban in May. And those attract international exhibitors, international visitors. If you look at the number of companies that are impacted by that, it's those businesses that are looking for a platform to grow their businesses and the different industry sectors, those businesses obviously affect the economy as a whole. So the ripple effect is enormous. Link: Parkhurst in Johannesburg is renowned as a social hub for restaurant, pub and coffee shop goers. On the eve of lockdown, it already feels like a dead zone as businesses prepare to shut down. VO: Restaurateur James Diack is closing his doors. He owns 4 eateries around Johannesburg. James: Just because our doors are shut, it doesn't mean that our costs have stopped We are a cash flow business, Claire: What have you communicated to your staff members, lots of anxiety going around? James: We've run a full payroll for this month. And then once we're back up and running, we will do our best to work with them we are all uncertain, we don't know where this ends. VO: Wendy Alberts, CEO of the Restaurant Association of South Africa has already been coordinating efforts to support the restaurant industry across the country. Wendy: Engagements that I'm going to have in the very next few days and weeks are gonna be very real conversations that we need to have with government and the landlords to put a financial plan relooking the entire financial ability of a lease agreement. Every restaurant will pay a percentage of turnover to the landlord. It means that the landlord is also playing a responsibility in driving feet through the doors in rebuilding their centers, in rebuilding those businesses. VO: Although the banks are coming to the party, with payment holidays for small businesses and student loans, there are more pressing issues for the man in the street, like rents, home loans and car repayments. Duma: I do not think we're going to see mass repossessions of people's cars and houses and so on. VO: Payment holidays for individual consumers have not yet been implemented, but some banks are encouraging customers to engage on a case by case basis. Albert Mashimbi owns one taxi and already he is not sure where his next paycheck is coming from. Albert: If normally in the morning the taxi takes three loads of people, it is no longer three loads. Just one load in the morning and one in the evening. We need to speak to the bank, so that our cars don't get taken Claire: Do you think your business will survive? Albert: No it’s not going to survive. VO: Philemon Mulaudzi, Chairperson of the Northern Taxi Liaison Committee is worried. Philemon: We don't have any plan. We will see if the government can assist us or maybe the government if they can talk to the banks. Maybe they can give us a little bit of money just to cover the cost over the months. VO: As global markets collapse under the strain of COVID-19, South Africa is not exempt from the fallout. Already in a recession and with foreign investment curtailed, now that Moody's has cut South Africa’s credit rating to junk, economic recovery could be even tougher. Duma: All the problems we have in society, they've just been fast forwarded in terms of you know the D-day for us as a country. So Eskom is going to have serious troubles over the next six months in terms of their financing. VO: On the plus side, with a slump in demand for electricity during lockdown, Eskom expects no load shedding and they are able to do short term maintenance and repairs to improve generation capacity. But other SOE's may fall by the wayside. Mike: There's no way that SAA or SA Express can survive under these circumstances. VO: And on Friday SA Express Business Rescue practitioners filed for liquidation. Mike: There might not even be a Prasa after this. So it's going to be a very sort of big social experiment that we've never seen before. Duma: We have to think innovatively So let's just say we're going to do an 800 billion stimulus. VO: According to Duma Gqubule the stimulus could come from various sources like foreign exchange reserves of about 800 billion rands, interest rate cuts, and surpluses in the Public Investment Corporation as well as the UIF. Duma : Let's look at the whole balance sheet of South Africa and not just focus on liabilities there's also the assets that we have as a country. VO: As the country locks down in eerie silence and shuts off for the next three weeks, how will one of the world's most unequal societies cope in unprecedented times?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Could the economic impact of coronavirus in South Africa be more deadly than the virus itself?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It is all good and well to declare Coronavirus a National Disaster and order business and people to stay at home and practice social distancing, but how is this going to affect small businesses and self employed people, who in South Africa are a major sector working class?
metadata.Summary: How is the imminent Lockdown and social distancing going to affect, the lives and livelihoods of South Africans. How is Coronavirus affecting the local economy and it’s impact on our current recession? What role is the National Command Council, set up as part of the national state of disaster, going to play in averting what could be disastrous for South Africa? It is all good and well to declare Coronavirus a National Disaster and order business and people to stay at home and practice social distancing, but how is this going to affect small businesses and self employed people, who in South Africa are a major sector working class? We look at the chain of employment and sustainability of workers that could potentially explode into an unimaginable situation. Experts say the economic impact of coronavirus could be more deadly than the virus itself. Restaurants now have regulated hours, they can’t have more than 40 people at a time, Parkhurst and Rosebank for example, on Saturday this week, were ghost towns. Waiters who work in these places depend on tips to make a living. If they are not going to work then the taxi industry is impacted, who also depend on fares to earn a wage for themselves and the taxi owners.
metadata.Further information: Driving around Johannesburg at the weekend, the city was lifeless. Gyms are closing down, many gym trainers pay the gym’s a monthly fee like R9000,00 per month, which they can only pay if they have clients to train. The Clients are freezing their gym accounts, but the trainers in some of these facilities are being asked to pay only 50% of their fees, but without clients, even this is not sustainable. There are people who depend on a living through weekly markets where they sell their wares, these markets are now being closed down. Those who are self employed are unable to sustain their businesses if they depend on client contact to earn money, eg, music teachers, etc.. We speak to people who’s incomes are already being compromised because of this, and it’s only the beginning. The question is, what happens when money starts running out, and people don’t have money to buy food, pay for electricity etc. Already people’s purses were stretched with the current recession and economic outlook. This could lead to looting and increased opportunistic crime, what is the Government Disaster fund doing to mitigate this? Have they set aside food packages that can be dropped off in areas where people may be starving, what is going to happen when people can’t afford to pay their electricity because their income has been stifled, how is Eskom’s current debt burden going to cope with this? We can try and get an interview with the President on this, who is the Chairperson of the Disaster Management Fund, or someone else that is suitable. Other countries like in the UK and Germany are allowing their citizens state help money, eg in Ireland they are receiving around $240 pounds a week, in South Africa we are in a recession with limited funds available for anything, the State cannot afford to help the ordinary citizen weather this storm, how is this going to play out in the poor communities who already have little if no assistance? Even criminals are going to find it harder to do certain crimes, with businesses closed down and people staying at home, it’s going to make burglaries harder, and therefore there may even be an increase in violent crime, even the amount of cars on the roads are reduced, and this will impede the way criminals operate which may give rise to a different type of crime wave. What is SAPS doing to secure communities in such eventualities? Mike Shussler warns, that the South African economy could shrink by a further 5% due to the measures taken around the world and in South Africa to combat the Covid 19 Pandemic, this would also lead to an increase in unemployment from an already high rate. Tourism in the Western Cape will be worst hit. The impact on Restaurants, hotels, Uber and Bolt drivers, thousands of people who normally make money for themselves may not be able to because of the pandemic. Wholesalers supplying to restaurants will take a hit, nursery schools will also lose money. The plus side of this is that pharmaceutical companies and food companies are flourishing. Professor Neil Rankin form Stellenbosch says, “real time data, suggests that sales are down by between 20% and 50% now, and that’s likely to get worse. “ There is also a prediction, that the worldwide impact could outdo the Great Depression of the 1920’s. This will affect South Africa even further because of our dependence on global economic links.
